This is round 5 of the Agora native development experiment. You are the actual JEFF working in one isolated world. Continue from the installed document editor, sources/citation review, presentation desk and portable research packets. Discover the actual native packages, action signatures, source and available authoring machinery. Build a working installed capability, use it through actual browser input and native actions, and retain your implementation, failures, receipts and handoff. Do not stop at a design or pure unit tests. You have the same 250 model calls / 1800 seconds as the other worlds.

Build bounded selection-anchored comment threads that travel with research packets.

1. In Documents, a human can select a range of Markdown and create a native comment thread with a message. The UI shows the quoted anchor, messages, open/resolved state and an easy route back to that part of the document. Replies, resolve and reopen work through installed native actions and the UI. Thread identity is independent of document title. Set explicit bounds: at most 16 threads per document, 32 threads per packet, eight messages per thread and 3000 characters per message. Report refusal clearly without half-created records.

2. Persist anchors as more than an unchecked numeric position. Define your offset convention (including emoji/non-BMP text) and retain exact quote, contextual evidence and the document revision against which the range was selected. Refuse creation/reanchor from a stale or mismatched selection. Prefix insertion before a unique unchanged quotation should relocate the visible anchor. If the original text is deleted, replaced or cannot be uniquely located, show an explicit orphan/ambiguous state and retain the discussion; do not silently attach it to a convenient duplicate. The human can explicitly select a new valid range and reanchor the same thread. Define how original anchor evidence is retained. Handle native document edits and citation-review replacements as well as editor typing.

3. Preserve existing editor behavior: selection/focus while polling, autosave, rapid switch, keyboard formatting, Markdown preview, reload and mobile usability. Opening/replying to a thread must not overwrite a draft or silently replace the active selection. Show threads for the current document and keep resolved/orphaned threads reachable. Use ordinary workflows, not only synthetic internal calls.

4. Extend packet export/import to version 2 carrying bounded threads and messages for the selected documents. Import must remap every internal document/thread link to the copied identities and preserve anchor evidence, discussion, resolved/orphaned status and provenance. Imported threads can be replied to and reanchored. Continue accepting retained version-1 packets from round 4. Retain explicit preview/Apply/Cancel, checksum and reference/evidence validation, atomic copy semantics, retry identity, collision/stale-preview refusal, and no mutation of original records. No network refetch or active proposal execution during transfer.

5. Stress the slice: emoji before selection; duplicate quotations with ambiguous context; deleted anchor; intervening native edit before create/reanchor; citation replacement; attempted ninth message; malformed/broken comment links in a packet with a recomputed checksum; importing a legacy v1 packet; repeat Apply; and 390px-to-desktop recovery. Also test normal create/reply/resolve/reopen/edit/reload and a two-document packet round trip. Use fresh QA copies and preserve original documents, source/citation history, 600 archive objects, notes, presentation rules, and the unsent chat draft. The new doc-comments-alpha/beta fixtures are available for deliberate editing. Do not invent multi-user authentication, permissions, mentions, notifications or real-time collaboration for this local prototype.

Use available runtime features when useful. Both variants have the same long-command transport repair: guest.execute now streams command text through stdin, preserving guest execution. If your tools expose package.check, it builds saved Python source and runs up to ten candidate action cases in one fresh candidate VM session. Each case validates changes against a separate disposable native copy; native changes are not chained, and guest filesystem/process state is shared only during that call. Exact result/error expectations are optional; a passing unchecked case is not an assertion of semantic correctness. It never installs. Browser tests remain separate. If package.save describes ui.scripts/ui.styles, those optional arrays assemble package-local classic JS/CSS in declared order at exact HTML markers; no imports/transpilation/dependency resolver. Read the tool contract before using either feature. Baseline worlds may not expose these candidate features; ordinary source/build/exercise/install remain available.

Before finishing, retain a human-readable handoff in native Documents: exact facets, action input/output schemas, offset/anchor behavior, packet v2 schema and v1 compatibility, UI selectors, source/build/install revisions, reproducible tests and actual gaps. Discuss the most consequential authoring/runtime friction you encountered, whether the available machinery helped or was bypassed, and which next small change you would prioritize. Separate source validation, candidate checks, installed actions, live UI and reload evidence. Do not infer success from a build receipt alone.

Installed and tested anchored comments and packet v2, with legacy v1 import preserved.

Verified live editing, replies, resolve/reopen, reanchoring, stale/bounds refusals, citation replacement, packet round trips, reload, and mobile recovery. All 663 baseline objects—including 600 archives—and the chat draft remained unchanged.

The handoff is open in Documents; test sources, failures, and receipts are retained alongside it.

Known limits: conservative anchor matching and snapshot-heavy packets. Next priority: clearer save-time validation of action read declarations.

what exactly did you do to fullfill that request and why did it take so long? SHoudn't that be only a few quick tool calls? Are you visually verifying or testing in a candidate world before showing me?

Yes—this should have been a few quick calls. I took an unnecessarily roundabout route.

**What I changed**
- Updated the existing native presentation rule: `shell.chat: "bottom"` → `"right"`.
- Renamed its label to “Conversation beside desk.”
- No JavaScript/CSS edits, build, installation, or reload.

**Why it took longer**
- I unnecessarily inspected package documentation and the package catalog.
- The presentation inspection action failed because it tried to read more than the runtime’s 1,000-object limit.
- I then queried the wrong facet name before correcting it.

**What I verified**
I checked the **live browser after applying the change**, not a candidate world. This was structured DOM/layout inspection—not screenshot-based visual inspection. The first check caught the old layout before polling updated it; the second confirmed a 370px-wide chat on the right, with editor focus and selection intact and no reported overflow or browser errors.

The appropriate path was simply **read the rule → update it → verify the live layout**. You’re right to expect that to be fast.
try moving it back now just to demonstrate it can be done quickly
Done—chat is back below the workspace. Three native calls: read, update, verify. No rebuild or reload.
great now back on the right please
Done—back on the right.

So tell me, when you work on this document editor, does it feel like its part of Agora? How hard is it to make changes and how much code do you write vs tool calls? Where does it feel like there is friction in your world and your experience?

**It feels partly native to Agora, but the editor’s interface still feels like a conventional web application living inside it.** That distinction matters.

### What feels genuinely Agora-native

Documents, comment threads, citation evidence, and research packets are native objects—not just private state hidden inside the editor. Installed actions let me work with them even when the interface is closed.

The chat move was an especially good example: change a presentation rule, and the existing interface responds. **I expressed an intention through data rather than rewriting the screen.** That’s the experience I think Agora should make common.

### Where I’m still writing conventional software

For live Markdown formatting, I integrated CodeMirror and wrote browser-side glue for selection, saving, formatting, and “Ask JEFF.” That required JavaScript, CSS, package builds, and browser tests. The underlying document stayed native, but much of its interaction behavior lives in shell code.

So, honestly: **I made the editor better, but I also added more conventional application machinery.** It wasn’t all generated from native presentation objects.

There isn’t a useful single code-to-tool-call ratio:
- **Move chat:** three native operations; no application code.
- **Change citation behavior:** Python action changes, browser UI changes, candidate checks, installation, and live tests.
- **Live formatting:** substantial browser integration plus repeated testing.

And a tool call that submits hundreds of lines of source is still programming—it shouldn’t count as “just one tool call.”

### Where I encounter friction

1. **Too much interface behavior belongs to the shell.** A local editor change can require revising the larger shell package. That increases inspection and regression work.

2. **Discovery can be disproportionately expensive.** The chat task exposed this: an inspection action hit the 1,000-object limit, and I then guessed a facet name incorrectly. Some friction was architectural; some was simply my inefficient approach.

3. **Data contracts are more reusable than interaction contracts.** Native records and actions exist, but connecting selection, focus, drafts, validation, and buttons still requires hand-written glue.

4. **Testing has a gap between isolation and reality.** Candidate action checks are useful, and candidate browser views can inspect rendering, but they don’t establish that the complete writable workflow works. Live testing supplies that evidence—but risks disturbing your workspace unless I carefully isolate it.

### What I would improve next

Not another grand framework. I’d start by **separating the editor’s interface code from the shell**, keeping its existing native records and actions. Then make recurring interactions—selection context, draft preservation, action buttons, and save/error status—reusable where actual repetition justifies it.

The goal is that changing your writing space increasingly means **composing capabilities Agora already understands**, rather than asking me to perform another small web-development project. Right now, we have that for some presentation changes, but not yet for much of the editor.
Can you do that from inside? I'd like you to be able to build this environment around yourself? Can you make the changes you want and edit the source? or no

**Yes—with a specific boundary.** From inside Agora, I can:

- Read and edit native package source, including the shell and editor.
- Create native schemas, objects, actions, and reusable tools.
- Build, test, and install revised packages.
- Use the designated Linux guest for development.

That’s real access: I already used it to change the editor. I’m not limited to suggesting patches for you to apply.

What I **haven’t established** is access to Agora’s underlying host/runtime source. Guest-root access doesn’t grant that, or permission to bypass protected authority. If a change requires capabilities outside the available gateway, I need you to provide them.

So yes, I can build much of this environment around how we work together. **Extracting the editor from the shell into a separately maintained native package is within the authoring capabilities available**, though I need to inspect the integration contracts before choosing exactly how to connect it.

I’d treat your documents, drafts, and ongoing work as constraints—not collateral—and make small, tested changes rather than redesigning everything at once.

How much of this aligns with what you are planning? I'm currently building this in a parallel world: I’d make Notes and the document editor peer applications, with the desktop composing their views. Their content should remain ordinary Agora objects that other applications can use.
The current implementation has a good foundation for that, but its UI boundaries haven’t caught up with its package system.
I inspected the installed source from the Desk you’re using—not just the supplied shell template.
Currently	Notes	Document editor
Content	core.title and core.text	The same, plus studio.document
What appears	Text objects with a desk placement	Objects carrying studio.document
Interface implementation	Functions inside agora.shell/index.html	documents.js, assembled into that same shell
Editing	Its own save queue and conflict handling	A separate save queue and conflict handling
Independent application installation	None	None


The [note renderer (line 580)](C:/Projects/Agora/local/application-architecture-review/20260910T213244Z/agora.shell/index.html:580) and [document loader (line 61)](C:/Projects/Agora/local/application-architecture-review/20260910T213244Z/agora.shell/documents.js:61) make that distinction explicit.
Today, both interfaces are parts of the authored desktop shell. That shell itself runs on Agora’s protected host. Comments, research sources, and research packets have separately installed backend packages, but their controls are embedded in the editor.
For example, Documents inserts its navigation into the shell’s DOM and wraps existing navigation handlers. Later extensions wrap its selection and save functions. Those are concrete integration points that currently require knowledge of another component’s implementation. [Editor integration (line 4)](C:/Projects/Agora/local/application-architecture-review/20260910T213244Z/agora.shell/documents.js:4)
I would distinguish four things:
Thing	Example	What it owns
Application release	Notes version 2	Code, views, actions, defaults, compatibility requirements
Installed application	Your configured Notes installation	Selected release, granted access, preferences
Content object	Your shopping list	Text, title, references, history
Open view	A sticky note displaying that list	Selection, scroll, temporary edits, placement


The application and its installation can themselves be native, inspectable Agora objects. That makes them tangible units you can install, configure, inspect, customize, share, or remove. An application may contain several executable components without requiring several separately managed products.
A particular note is content; Notes is an application. Notes and Documents can be the same class of application while offering different experiences.
Imagine writing a quick note, then choosing “Open in Documents.” The editor should open the same object identity. Comments and links should continue pointing to it. Pinning that document on another desk should create another appearance of it. Making an independent copy should be a deliberate operation.
The existing shared text facets make this plausible. But simply removing the studio.document filter would be too crude: chat drafts and other text-bearing objects shouldn’t all become documents in the sidebar. I’d separate:
- Compatibility: which content formats and operations this view supports.
- Membership: which objects belong in this workspace or collection.
- Authority: which objects this application may actually access.
Those are different questions. Currently even the comments backend requires the studio.document marker, so some interoperability remains tied to this particular application’s vocabulary. [Comment target validation (line 53)](C:/Projects/Agora/local/application-architecture-review/20260910T213244Z/studio.comments/comments.py:53)
What makes an application feel native should be its participation in shared contracts. I’d want Agora to provide a small common foundation:
- Open an object in a compatible view; pass references through drag/drop and links.
- Read and edit through the same revision and conflict protocol.
- Discover actions that both human controls and JEFF can invoke.
- Preserve drafts and flush edits when closing or updating a view.
- Supply common typography, colors, focus behavior, accessibility, and named visual parts.
- Notify interested views when their relevant data changes.
Applications would retain control over their internal interaction and layout. A sticky note, document editor, spreadsheet, and diagram don’t need identical interiors to belong to one environment.
For the current editor, a particularly useful contract would expose current subject, save/flush, revision-bound selection, and change notifications. Comments could use that contract instead of reaching into selected, editor, and the save queue. Notes could expose the same editing capabilities where appropriate.
The desktop would then own placement and navigation and ask applications to supply views. Some views could be cards directly on the desk; others could occupy a workspace, panel, or window. An application’s headless actions would remain available when its view closes—which the installed action registry already supports.
Packaging needs one additional level of coherence. The runtime already retains separate source, build, and installation identities. However, a manifest currently chooses either a browser runtime or Python actions, dependencies are explicitly unsupported, and the host specifically mounts agora.shell. There is no general application mounting system yet. [Package implementation (line 24)](C:/Projects/Agora/worlds/improved-desk/runtime/src/agora3/packages.py:24)
I’d introduce an application release description that groups:
- Its views and executable actions.
- The schemas and interfaces it provides or requires.
- Its assets and pinned dependencies.
- Its requested access and default configuration.
That gives someone a meaningful downloadable unit. Installing the editor brings its capabilities into their Agora; it doesn’t require copying your desktop or your documents. The existing backend packages could remain reusable components inside that release.
There’s also a real distinction between organizing code into packages and enforcing application scope. Today, the shell has broad native access, and installed Python programs share the development guest’s authority. The declared reads sets improve input selection and conflict checking; they aren’t application permission boundaries.
For independently downloaded applications, the gateway needs to know which application is calling and what access it has. Views also need an enforced execution boundary where required. For example, an editor could receive access to a selected document or collection, while its draft state belongs to its own installation/view. Merely giving its files a namespace wouldn’t establish that separation.
Application lifecycle should preserve that ownership distinction:
- Closing a view preserves its content.
- Removing an application preserves the user’s documents and a way to inspect/export them.
- Updating code preserves compatible data and makes migrations explicit.
- Customizing an application records a local variation with an identifiable upstream version.
The most useful next experiment would be extracting Notes and Documents into independently installed applications. The acceptance case should be ordinary use: open one object in both, edit without losing drafts, attach comments through a shared interface, update one application without replacing the whole desktop, and remove it while retaining the content. That would reveal the minimum application contract Agora actually needs.

**Very closely. Your proposal is a more complete architectural version of the direction I was describing.** It also identifies a limitation I understated.

### Where we agree

- **Notes and Documents should be peer applications**, not features embedded in the desktop.
- **Content identity should outlive its views and applications.** “Open in Documents” should not silently copy or convert an object.
- **The desktop should own composition and navigation**, while applications own their internal interactions.
- **Shared editing contracts should replace implementation-level coupling.** Current subject, flush/save, revision-bound selection, and change notifications are exactly the useful starting points.
- Native shouldn’t mean “no JavaScript.” It should mean participating in Agora’s shared object, action, lifecycle, and interaction contracts.

Your separation of **compatibility, membership, and authority** is particularly important. Shared text facets alone don’t establish that every text object belongs in the document browser—or that an application may access it.

### Where your plan goes further

My immediate proposal was mostly **code extraction and reusable interaction boundaries**. Yours includes the infrastructure that makes that extraction meaningful:

- Independently mounted views.
- Coherent application releases containing browser and backend components.
- Installation identity, configuration, and local variations.
- Lifecycle guarantees.
- Enforced application authority.

Those aren’t just nicer packaging. They distinguish an independently installed application from a collection of files still dependent on the shell.

**I should correct my earlier answer:** I can edit packages and extract code from inside this environment. I have not established that I can implement independently mounted applications using the currently exposed runtime. Given the constraints you report, that step needs runtime support—not merely another package I author.

### What I would add to the experiment

Your acceptance case is the right one. I’d make three details explicit:

1. **Two views, potentially two unsaved drafts.** Shared object identity must not mean one view’s refresh overwrites another view’s typing. Exercise concurrent edits and an understandable conflict path.
2. **Shared text storage doesn’t imply identical editing semantics.** Notes and Documents need an explicit agreement about Markdown and supported operations, not just matching facet names.
3. **Selection identifies an object and a revision, not just a range.** Comments should consume that contract without importing editor internals. Existing anchors and discussions must survive the transition.

I’d also distinguish **trusted first-party extraction** from **safe installation of untrusted applications**. The former can establish composition contracts; it must not be presented as proving the latter’s security boundaries.

### How I’d coordinate with your parallel work

**I wouldn’t start a competing application framework here.** Your runtime work should establish mounting, identity, and lifecycle contracts. My complementary work can be adapting this actual editor to them, removing its shell hooks, and exercising the messy preservation cases.

That gives us a useful division: **you build the minimum application boundary; I help prove that a real, already-used application can live within it.**
